pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Types of Teeth

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans'):** "identify the different types of teeth in humans and their simple functions".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE):** No NGSS elementary PE names human tooth types; the nearest structure-for-function idea is 4-LS1-1 (structures that support survival), and teeth appear illustratively in comparisons of animal diets. Treat as UK-led.

- **Operational details:** Children learn the four tooth types by SHAPE→FUNCTION: incisors (front, chisel-shaped, for biting/cutting), canines (pointed, for tearing/gripping), premolars and molars (broad, ridged, back teeth for chewing/grinding). This connects to the digestive-system topic (teeth are the first, mechanical stage of digestion) and to diet: a carnivore has large canines for tearing meat; a herbivore has broad molars for grinding plants; humans, as omnivores, have all types. Also cover simple tooth care (the reason for brushing) as an applied extension. Best explored by feeling one's own teeth with the tongue and mapping shape to job.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A Y4 child can name the four types, locate them in their own mouth, and match each shape to its job; the small conceptual stretch is linking tooth shape to an animal's diet (carnivore vs herbivore) as evidence, rather than treating teeth as arbitrary.
bestPractices: Start with the child's own mouth: run the tongue over front, side and back teeth and notice the different shapes before naming them, so the categories are felt.
Teach each type as SHAPE→FUNCTION (chisel incisor cuts, pointed canine tears, broad molar grinds) rather than as a list of names to memorise.
Use animal-jaw comparisons (carnivore vs herbivore vs omnivore) so children see tooth shape as EVIDENCE of diet, deepening the shape-function link.
Explicitly connect teeth to the digestive system topic — teeth are the first, mechanical breakdown stage — so the two Y4 topics reinforce each other.
Add applied tooth-care (why we brush, what causes decay) as a motivating real-world hook, but keep it distinct from the naming objective.
Have children count and locate their own tooth types with a mirror to make the count and arrangement concrete.
keyRepresentations: A labelled human jaw diagram with the four tooth types colour-coded
A shape→job strip pairing each tooth silhouette with the food action it performs (bite/tear/grind)
Comparison of a carnivore, herbivore and omnivore jaw showing how tooth proportions match diet
A mirror-and-count activity mapping the child's own teeth
A cross-link to the digestive-system 'mouth' stage showing teeth as step one of digestion
commonMisconceptions: Thinking all teeth are basically the same, missing that shape determines function.
Believing canines are for 'being fierce' rather than tearing/gripping food, or that humans lack them.
Assuming only meat-eaters have sharp teeth and plant-eaters have none, rather than each diet favouring particular tooth proportions.
Treating teeth as unrelated to digestion, rather than as its first mechanical stage.
Confusing premolars and molars, or thinking baby teeth and adult teeth have different jobs.

learn.summary: Children aged 8–9 learn the four human tooth types by reasoning from SHAPE to FUNCTION: incisors (front, chisel-shaped, bite/cut), canines (pointed, tear/grip), premolars and molars (broad, ridged, chew/grind). They start from their own mouth, map each shape to its job, then use animal-jaw comparisons to see tooth shape as evidence of diet (carnivore, herbivore, omnivore), and connect teeth to the first mechanical stage of digestion. Activities span first-hand exploration, a labelled-jaw reveal, shape-to-job sorting, diet inference from skulls, consolidation checks, and an optional dentist conversation for tooth-care motivation.

activities.title: Feel and map your own teeth
feedback: If a learner thinks all teeth do the same job or that only the front teeth are used, have them notice which teeth bite versus which chew the apple: incisors cut, molars grind.
Confirm the felt categories: chisel front teeth for cutting, pointed teeth for tearing/gripping, broad back teeth for grinding.
activities.rationale: Starting from the child's own mouth makes the categories concrete and felt before names are attached, and a predict-then-observe apple task directly challenges the 'all teeth are the same' misconception. The underlying fact that the different types have distinct jobs is the source-grounded content.
sourceClaims: Human tooth types and simple functions: incisors bite/cut, canines tear/grip, premolars and molars chew/grind; tooth shape relates to diet (carnivore canines, herbivore molars, omnivore has all).
learnerActions: Run your tongue over the front, side and back teeth and notice the different shapes before naming them.

Using a mirror, count and locate each tooth type (counts will differ between children at this age because baby teeth are still being replaced and some may be missing): flat chisel-shaped front teeth, pointed teeth beside them, and broad bumpy teeth at the back.
Say aloud which teeth feel sharp/chisel-like and which feel broad, and guess what each shape might be good for.

Bite a firm apple: predict first which teeth you'll use for the first bite and which for chewing, and why; then notice which teeth you actually use — usually the front incisors for the first bite, then the apple is moved to the broad back teeth to grind (a child with missing front teeth may bite with side teeth instead).
activities.intendedInsight: Even within one mouth, different teeth have different shapes and do different jobs — teeth are not all the same.

activities.title: Labelled jaw: tap to reveal shape and job
feedback: When a learner matches a type to its job correctly, affirm the shape-reason (pointed = tear, broad = grind), not just the name.
If canines are described as being 'for being fierce', redirect: pointed canines tear and grip food, and humans have them too.
activities.rationale: This is a naming-and-function topic anchored to fixed mouth structures; a labelled diagram with highlight-and-reveal pairs each shape→function fact with its location. The highlighting and flap interactions make the shape-function pairing concrete, though a static labelled diagram with a shape→job strip can also convey the same content.
sourceClaims: Human tooth types and simple functions: incisors bite/cut, canines tear/grip, premolars and molars chew/grind; tooth shape relates to diet (carnivore canines, herbivore molars, omnivore has all).
learnerActions: On a labelled human jaw diagram, tap each of the four tooth types; tapping a type highlights all instances of it.

Read the revealed shape→function for each: incisor 'chisel-shaped — bites and cuts, like biting into an apple'; canine 'pointed — tears and grips'; premolars and molars 'broad and bumpy — chew and grind'.
Open myth-buster flaps such as 'are all teeth the same?' and 'why does a dog have such big canines?' and 'what are wisdom teeth?'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each named tooth type has a characteristic shape that matches a specific food action; names and functions go together.

activities.title: Match tooth shape to the food job
feedback: If a learner pairs a broad molar with tearing, point to the flat ridged surface — good for grinding, not for cutting into flesh.
Reinforce correct pairings by restating the shape reason so the match is not just memorised.
activities.rationale: Active matching gives a shape-to-function workout that applies the naming to food actions; it complements rather than replaces first teaching of the names.
sourceClaims: Human tooth types and simple functions: incisors bite/cut, canines tear/grip, premolars and molars chew/grind; tooth shape relates to diet (carnivore canines, herbivore molars, omnivore has all).
learnerActions: Drag each tooth type onto the food action it handles: incisor → biting an apple, canine → tearing meat, molar → grinding grain.
Explain in one sentence why that shape suits that action.
Build a shape→job strip pairing each tooth silhouette with its food action (bite / tear / grind).
activities.intendedInsight: Tooth shape is functional: the chisel cuts, the point tears, the broad ridged surface grinds.

activities.title: Read a skull's diet from its teeth
feedback: If a learner says you can't tell diet from teeth, or that all animals have much the same teeth, compare a cat skull and a sheep skull directly: sharp tearing teeth vs broad grinding teeth — tooth shape is a reliable clue to diet.
If a learner reasons from how big or fierce the animal looks, redirect to function: pointed = tear, flat = grind; a large horse has broad flat back teeth for grinding plants despite its size.
Note that plant-eaters are not toothless and meat-eaters are not the only ones with sharp teeth — each diet favours particular tooth proportions.
activities.rationale: Animal-jaw comparison lets children treat tooth shape as evidence of diet, deepening the shape-function link and distinguishing diet from size/fierceness. The diagnostic skull prompt discriminates learners who reason shape→function→diet from those who cannot infer or who reason from size.
sourceClaims: Human tooth types and simple functions: incisors bite/cut, canines tear/grip, premolars and molars chew/grind; tooth shape relates to diet (carnivore canines, herbivore molars, omnivore has all).
learnerActions: Compare a carnivore, herbivore and omnivore jaw side by side, noticing how tooth proportions differ (large canines and few flat teeth vs broad grinding molars with small or no canines vs a mix of pointed canines and broad flat back teeth).
Play 'whose skull?': match predator and herbivore jaws to diets by their teeth.
Answer: a scientist finds a skull with long pointed teeth at the front and hardly any broad flat teeth at the back — would it eat mostly meat or mostly plants, and what about the teeth tells you?

Discuss: a big grizzly bear and a small pet cat both eat meat and both have sharp canines (the bear also eats lots of plants and has broader back teeth) — is it size that decides tooth shape, or diet? And why would a cow or horse need broad flat teeth at the back?
activities.intendedInsight: Tooth shape is evidence of diet in both directions: you can name a tooth's job, and you can infer an animal's diet from an unfamiliar skull. Large pointed tearing teeth with few broad flat grinding teeth suggest a meat-eater; many broad flat ridged back teeth suggest a plant-eater.

activities.title: Teeth as the first step of digestion
feedback: If a learner treats teeth as unrelated to digestion, point out that chewing is the first step that breaks food up before it moves on to the stomach.
Keep tooth-care discussion distinct: it motivates care but does not change the names and jobs of the four tooth types.
activities.rationale: Explicitly linking teeth to digestion reinforces both Y4 topics, and applied tooth-care provides a motivating hook while being kept distinct from the naming objective. Neither source directly states the digestion cross-link or tooth-care content, so no source claim is cited.
learnerActions: Trace the 'mouth' stage of the digestive system, describing teeth as the first, mechanical breakdown of food before it travels on.
Explain how biting, tearing and grinding each prepare food for swallowing.
As an applied extension, discuss why we brush and what causes tooth decay, keeping this separate from naming the tooth types.
activities.intendedInsight: Teeth are not isolated — they are the first mechanical stage of digestion, connecting the teeth topic to the digestive-system topic; tooth care is a real-world application.

activities.title: Consolidate and check understanding
feedback: Full understanding: reasons shape→function→diet in both directions — names each job and infers an unfamiliar skull's diet.
Partial understanding: names the tooth types and their jobs but cannot yet confidently infer an unknown animal's diet from its teeth — revisit the skull-comparison activity.
Gap: cannot connect tooth shape to function or diet, or reasons from size/fierceness — return to feeling own teeth and the cat-vs-sheep skull comparison.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorisation and diet-reasoning questions assess the topic fully; these consolidate and check rather than first-teach. On their own, recognition-style matching does not elicit the first-hand noticing or independent inference, so pair them with explanation.
sourceClaims: Human tooth types and simple functions: incisors bite/cut, canines tear/grip, premolars and molars chew/grind; tooth shape relates to diet (carnivore canines, herbivore molars, omnivore has all).
learnerActions: Match each tooth type to its job, and sort teeth into biting / tearing / grinding categories.
Answer a question such as 'which teeth would be especially large and important in a lion's mouth, and why?' giving the shape reason.
Explain in your own words why a herbivore needs broad flat back teeth and a carnivore needs large pointed canines.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands the topic can both name each tooth's job and infer diet from teeth, reasoning from shape to function to diet.

activities.title: Optional: ask a dentist (enrichment)
feedback: Encourage follow-up questions that press on the shape-reason ('why pointed? why broad?') rather than stopping at the name.
Use this as motivation; still confirm the four names and jobs through one of the core activities.
activities.rationale: A dentist persona offers a plausible enrichment route that may motivate the shape-function link and tooth care through curiosity, though it is not the most direct route to the naming objective and its efficacy is untested.
learnerActions: In a short in-role conversation with a dentist, ask why front and back teeth are different, why molars are at the back, and what happens if you don't brush.
Use the dentist's answers to connect tooth shape, function and tooth care through your own questions.
activities.intendedInsight: Curiosity-led questions can motivate the shape-function link and tooth care, framing the facts around the child's own 'why' questions.

constraints: Target age 8–9 (UK DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans'). No NGSS elementary performance expectation names human tooth types; the nearest US structure-for-function idea is 4-LS1-1, with teeth appearing illustratively in animal-diet comparisons — treat as UK-led.
Teach each type as SHAPE→FUNCTION rather than as a list of names to memorise.
Keep applied tooth-care distinct from the naming objective so it motivates without replacing the core content.

Matching, sorting and multiple-choice checks consolidate and assess classification, but do not by themselves elicit the first-hand noticing of one's own teeth or the independent inference of diet from an unfamiliar skull; pair recognition tasks with explanation or construction.

A labelled 2D jaw is sufficient for this age; a rotatable 3D mouth is not required to meet the naming and shape-to-function objective. This is a scope note for this topic, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing.
The myth-buster flaps and highlight-on-tap are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second source (BBC Bitesize) is marked verified:false in the row; its diet/tooth-shape claim is widely taught but was not independently re-checked here.

The DfE statutory claim states the topic/learning objective rather than a teaching principle, so it is not cited as a per-activity sourceClaim; the digestion cross-link and tooth-care extension are not directly supported by either source.
The original row's 'evidence' and parent 'description' list only three tooth types (incisors, canines, molars), omitting premolars; this guidance teaches all four, which is the correct human set.

Real tooth proportions vary by species; carnivore/herbivore/omnivore comparisons are generalisations. Use clear contrasting exemplars (e.g. cat vs sheep) and avoid implying plant-eaters have no sharp teeth or that only meat-eaters have canines.
The original row's 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' fit rankings and product-type labels have been removed; alternatives are preserved as distinct activities by pedagogical purpose rather than ranked.

assess.poeTask: Give each child a firm apple. Ask them to PREDICT which teeth they'll use for the first bite and which for chewing, and why. Biting with the front incisors and then shifting the apple to the back molars to grind challenges the idea that all teeth do the same job.
probeDeeper: Why would a plant-eater like a cow or horse need broad flat teeth at the back?
A big grizzly bear and a small pet cat both have sharp canines — so is it size that decides tooth shape, or diet?
Which of your own teeth would you use to bite an apple, and which to chew it?
If you found a skull with only flat, ridged teeth, what would you guess it ate, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: Mostly meat (a carnivore): long pointed canines are for gripping and tearing flesh, and the broad flat molars used to grind tough plants are missing or reduced, so it isn't built to grind vegetation. Tooth shape matches the animal's diet.

errorPatterns.pattern: You can't tell what an animal eats from its teeth — teeth are all much the same
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a cat skull and a sheep skull: sharp tearing teeth vs broad grinding teeth. Tooth shape is a reliable clue to diet.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't tell what an animal eats just from its teeth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the skull gives no clue to diet, or that all animals have basically the same teeth

errorPatterns.pattern: Sharp or big teeth just mean a fiercer or bigger animal, not a particular diet
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect from size/fierceness to function: pointed = tear, flat = grind. A big herbivore (horse) has flat teeth despite its size.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sharp teeth just mean it's a big, dangerous animal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasons from how dangerous or large the animal looks rather than what the teeth are shaped to do

errorPatterns.pattern: All our teeth do the same job / we use only our front teeth
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them notice which teeth they use to bite versus chew; different teeth do different jobs even in one mouth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats human teeth as interchangeable rather than incisors cutting, canines tearing, molars grinding

responseLevels.gap: Cannot connect tooth shape to function or diet; thinks teeth are all alike or reasons from size/fierceness.
responseLevels.full: Reasons shape→function→diet in both directions — naming each tooth's job and inferring an animal's diet from an unfamiliar skull.
responseLevels.partial: Names the tooth types and their jobs but can't confidently infer an unknown animal's diet from its teeth.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A scientist finds a skull with long pointed teeth at the front and hardly any broad flat teeth at the back. Would you expect this animal to eat mostly meat or mostly plants — and what is it about the teeth that tells you?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands shape→function→diet reasons from the pointed tearing teeth and absent grinders to a meat diet. A child without it can't infer diet from teeth, or reasons from size/fierceness rather than shape.
